title: Home Assistant Rebrands Cloud Service as “Link,” Boosting Smart Home Integration Options
body:
The open‑source smart‑home platform Home Assistant announced today that its subscription‑based service, formerly known as Home Assistant Cloud, will be rebranded as “Home Assistant Link.” The change, explained by founder and CEO Paulus Schoutsen, reflects a strategic shift away from the term “cloud” toward a broader vision that includes a new hardware hub and AI‑driven automation agents, positioning the ecosystem for wider consumer adoption.

Schoutsen said the word “cloud” no longer captures the service’s evolving role. While the original cloud offering primarily provided remote access, voice‑assistant integration and easy connection to third‑party services, the revamped Link will act as a connective layer that unifies on‑premises devices, edge computing resources and emerging AI capabilities. “We wanted a name that conveys continuity and integration rather than a location,” he explained during a virtual press briefing. “Link is about bridging the gap between local control and the intelligent services that users expect.”

The rebranding coincides with the imminent launch of Home Assistant Hub, a compact, purpose‑built gateway that runs the core Home Assistant software on a dedicated processor. Unlike the previous reliance on generic Raspberry Pi or Docker deployments, the Hub promises a plug‑and‑play experience, with built‑in Zigbee, Matter, Thread and Wi‑Fi radios, plus a secure enclave for encrypted communications. Early testers report faster device discovery and more reliable local automation, addressing long‑standing concerns about latency and reliability in cloud‑centric setups.

Perhaps the most ambitious component of the Link rollout is the introduction of AI agents that can learn user habits, suggest automations and even respond to natural‑language queries without routing data through external servers. By leveraging on‑device inference models, Home Assistant aims to keep personal data within the home while still offering the convenience of voice assistants. Schoutsen highlighted that the AI layer will be optional and configurable, allowing privacy‑focused users to disable any cloud interaction entirely.

Industry analysts see the move as a response to growing consumer wariness about data privacy and the dominance of big tech platforms in the smart‑home market. “Home Assistant has always been the go‑to for hobbyists and power users, but scaling that to mainstream households requires a more polished hardware offering and a clear value proposition that doesn’t rely on opaque cloud services,” noted Maya Patel, senior analyst at TechInsights. “If Link can deliver seamless AI features while maintaining local‑first privacy, it could carve out a significant niche between DIY enthusiasts and proprietary ecosystems like Amazon Alexa or Google Home.”

The rebranding also signals a shift in the company’s revenue model. While the core Home Assistant software remains free and open source, Link will continue as a subscription service, now bundling remote access, premium AI agents, and priority support for Hub owners. Schoutsen assured existing subscribers that pricing will stay unchanged for the next twelve months, with a gradual rollout of new features to justify future price adjustments.

Looking ahead, Home Assistant’s leadership hopes that Link and the Hub will accelerate adoption among users who have been hesitant to commit to a fully cloud‑based solution. By emphasizing edge computing, privacy‑preserving AI and a unified naming scheme, the company aims to position itself as the bridge between the open‑source community and the mainstream smart‑home market. If the new hardware and AI agents live up to their promises, Home Assistant could become a pivotal player in the next generation of connected homes, offering an alternative that blends flexibility, security and intelligent automation under a single, cohesive brand.
